After completing a project with Copilot, however, students felt that Copilot requires a competent programmer to complete some tasks manually." (2) Sec 3.3: "We do not use acceptance rate to measure trust since acceptance rate is a behavior, which is different from treating trust as an attitude [4]." date_and_recency: Posted to arXiv 16 Sep 2025. Data collected in a course that began April 2025 (VS Code 1.99): lecture surveys (pre/post, same 80-minute session) and a final survey at submission of a roughly 10-day project.
key_claims: Trust is dynamic. Self-reported trust went up after a short lecture with Copilot demos and a small task, then more students reported trust falling after a 10-day brownfield feature project. After extended use the dominant theme was that Copilot 'requires a competent programmer' to find, comprehend, debug or complete parts of the task. Reasons for rising trust: seeing correct output, context awareness, understanding how the tool works (NLP basics), learning its features. Main reason for falling trust: incorrect output. Authors recommend educators let students use assistants on tasks of varied difficulty, keep teaching comprehension, debugging and testing without AI so students can verify output, explain NLP basics, and demo features.
headline_figures: Immediate (after ~1h lecture, n=71) self-reported trust change: 49.3% increased, 33.8% no change, 16.9% decreased. Extended (after 10-day project): 39.4% increased, 23.9% no change, 36.6% decreased. Chi-square test of trend p = 0.03. Among those whose trust rose immediately, 48.6% rose again and 40.0% fell after the project. Prior experience, immediate use: 60.0% of no-experience students increased vs 38.9% of experienced (not significant). Extended: 38.9% vs 40.0% increased. 6-item survey (1-5 scale, Amoozadeh et al.): pre-survey means below 3.0; significant rises (paired t-test, Holm-Bonferroni) for S3 'I know what will happen the next time I use GitHub Copilot because I understand how it behaves' and S5 'personal preference' after the lecture, and S2 'output as good as a highly competent person could produce' after the project. Notably no significant change on S1 'I trust GitHub Copilot's output' or S6 'Overall, I trust' reported in text. Themes after extended use: 'requires a competent programmer' 36.6% of all responses; 'depends on quality of prompts' 15.5%; among decreased-trust students (n=26) 54% cited incorrect output and 54% needed a competent programmer; among increased-trust students (n=28) 57% cited correct output. 87% had no prior Copilot experience on large code bases; 49.3% had never used Copilot.
sample_unit_and_population: 71 upper-division CS students (one advanced brownfield software engineering elective at UC San Diego, large US public university) who completed all three surveys. Demographics from only 60 of them (80% Asian/Asian-American, 67% he/him, 57% no internship). Code base: idlelib from CPython, about 23,500 lines in 128 files. Task: add a 'Go to Definition' feature, roughly 30 lines, using Copilot. Student, not professional, population; single course, single term. Qualitative coding n=36 (prior experience question), n=35/12 (immediate up/down), n=28/17/26 (extended up/same/down).
observed_vs_stated: Entirely stated/self-reported. Data are Likert survey items plus open-ended free text and a self-assessed 'did your trust increase/no/decrease' question. The authors explicitly did not measure behaviour (no acceptance rate, no logs of accepted/rejected suggestions, no verification behaviour). The competent-programmer theme is students describing their own manual work, not an observed measurement.
what_makes_trust_justified: Authors treat calibrated trust as the goal, not high trust. Trust judgments should rest on the student's ability to verify output: 'students can still comprehend, modify, debug, and test code in large code bases without AI assistants' (Rec. 2). Also exposure to tasks of varied difficulty (Rec. 1), understanding how the tool generates output (Rec. 3), and knowing its features (Rec. 4). Frames via MATCH model (trustworthiness attributes, affordances, judgments). Not a claim that any specific control makes agent output safe.
what_it_costs: Not quantified. Implied costs: the programmer must find, comprehend and debug code manually when Copilot fails; students re-prompted and modified prompts ('depends on quality of prompts'); maintaining non-AI verification skills. No time or review-burden measurements.
failure_mode_class: Wrong code (incorrect output, failure to locate the right file, inability to debug its own code, handle edge cases) and over-/under-reliance as the framing risk. The paper cites Perry et al. for insecure code with false confidence but does not itself test security.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study; none applicable. The closest is the recommended human verification skill (comprehend, debug, test without AI).
limitations_stated: Attitude not behaviour: 'we only investigate students' trust as an attitude ... rather than as a behavior'. Findings limited to students with similar backgrounds, a Python code base of roughly 23,000 lines. 10 days only: 'we cannot extrapolate our findings to a longer time frame'. Threats: instructor endorsement heuristic may have skewed responses; surveys may prime students to reflect on trust. Author-listed additional caveat: 11 of 71 had no demographics.
counter_evidence: The trust story is mixed rather than a monotone rise: net immediate rise was followed by 36.6% reporting decline after extended use. Trust did not rise on the headline 'I trust Copilot's output' item per the text (only S2, S3, S5 flagged), so 'trust increased' rests partly on self-assessed change question. Prior experienced students showed smaller, non-significant immediate rises. Authors' own reading of the immediate rise is confounded by lecture priming and instructor endorsement. Related work they cite: Amoozadeh et al. found upper-division students less trusting than CS2 students; Brown et al. found early-career developers accept more AI suggestions.

usable_claim: In a 2025 survey study of 71 upper-division CS students at one US university, more students reported trust in GitHub Copilot rising than falling after a one-hour introduction (49.3% vs 16.9%), but after a 10-day project on a 23,500-line legacy code base 36.6% reported falling trust, and the most common reason given was that Copilot needed a competent programmer to finish or fix the work. All of this is self-reported attitude, not observed behaviour.
do_not_use: Do not present as evidence about professional developers, agents, or long-run trust. Do not say trust 'increased' without noting the survey items and self-assessed question differ and the 10-day result tilted downward. Do not present the 'competent programmer' theme as a measured verification burden or cost. Do not imply acceptance rates, verification behaviour or defect rates were observed. Do not say the paper shows verification practices work.
